metadata.title: Uniform Random Planar Graphs with Degree Constraints

extraction_notes.note: The thesis writes proofs as \textbf{Proof} ... picture-box qed; the facts' proof spans run past the qed to the next environment, so these proof nodes also contain the following lead-in sentences. \refs that occur only after the qed were added as mention edges.

These results have no proof of their own: a lead-in sentence ('Lemma 18 provides us with...', 'We may now combine...') justifies them, but that sentence lies inside another proof's span. The dependency is recorded as uses edges (proves for Proposition 33) instead of separate proof nodes.

The prompt asks for rigor: semi_formal on proof sketches, but the schema and the finishing step allow rigor on no proof. The 13 'Sketch of Proof' nodes therefore carry no rigor field; their proves edges carry alternative: true, and the 'Full Proof' is the main proof.

The Section 18 algorithm spans many sub-subsections. It is given as a sketch algorithm plus one algorithm node per subsection (Stage 4 overview, initialisation, iterative loop, cases). Stage 1-3 correctness arguments are claim+proof pairs, and the structural preambles of cases (a) and (b) are remarks.

The summary tables (Part I component/connectivity/subgraph results, the kappa summary and the Part II 'Summary of Results') restate results with \refs in tabular form. They are not extracted as nodes.
Retyped from example to claim: Example 94 asserts that no 4-regular planar graph contains K5 minus an edge, and the following proof proves it.
Conjecture or external theorem: one sentence both cites the result of [mcd2] (max degree of order log n) and conjectures its extension. It cannot be split, so it is typed conjecture.
The sentence stating the cited planarity result also defines 'asymptotically almost surely'. Because a sentence cannot be split, a.a.s. has no definition node of its own.

nodes.name: Random graph with edge probability p
nodes.statement: The \textit{random graph with edge probability $p$} is the random graph on the vertex set $\{ 1,2, \ldots, n \}$ where each of the $\left( ^{n}_{2} \right)$ possible edges occur independently with probability $p=p(n)$.
nodes.genus: random graph on the vertex set $\{ 1,2, \ldots, n \}$
differentia: each of the $\left( ^{n}_{2} \right)$ possible edges occur independently with probability $p=p(n)$

nodes.name: Uniform random graph with m edges
nodes.statement: By contrast, the \textit{uniform random graph with $m$ edges} is the graph taken uniformly at random from among all the graphs on $\{ 1,2, \ldots, n \}$ that have \textit{exactly} $m=m(n)$ edges.

nodes.name: Random graph process
nodes.statement: An alternative way to define the uniform random graph with $m$ edges is via the \textit{random graph process}, where one starts at stage zero with an empty graph and inserts all $\left( ^{n}_{2} \right)$ edges one by one in a (uniformly) random order.

nodes.name: Connectivity threshold for the random graph
nodes.statement: For example, it is known that $n^{-1} \log n$ is a `threshold' for the property that a random graph with edge probabilty $\!p$ will be connected, meaning that \begin{displaymath} \mathbf{P} [\textrm{connected}] \to \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0 & \textrm{if $\frac{np(n)}{\log n} \to 0 \textrm{ as } n \to \infty$} \\ 1 & \textrm{if $\frac{np(n)}{\log n} \to \infty \textrm{ as } n \to \infty$.} \end{array} \right. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: $n^{-1}\log n$ is the connectivity threshold of the random graph with edge probability $p$.
conclusions: $n^{-1} \log n$ is a `threshold' for the property that a random graph with edge probabilty $\!p$ will be connected

nodes.name: Planar graph
nodes.statement: A graph is said to be \textit{planar} if it is possible to draw it in the plane (or, equivalently, on the sphere) in such a way that the edges do not cross, meeting only at vertices.

nodes.name: Class P(n) of planar graphs
nodes.statement: Throughout this thesis, we shall use $\mathcal{P}(n)$ to denote the class of all planar graphs on the vertex set $\{ 1,2, \ldots, n \}$.

nodes.name: Maximum size of a planar graph
nodes.statement: It can be shown that, for $n \geq 3$, the maximum number of edges of a graph in $\mathcal{P}(n)$ is $3n-6$, so $K_{5}$, for example, cannot be planar, since it has $10$ edges.
conclusions: the maximum number of edges of a graph in $\mathcal{P}(n)$ is $3n-6$

nodes.name: Triangulation
nodes.statement: The maximum size (where we use `size' to mean the number of edges) is achieved if and only if a graph is a \textit{triangulation}, i.e.~if and only if it is possible to draw the graph in the plane in such a way that each face, including the outside face, is a triangle.

nodes.name: Extension to a triangulation
nodes.statement: It is always possible to extend a planar graph to a triangulation by inserting extra edges.
conclusions: It is always possible to extend a planar graph to a triangulation by inserting extra edges.

nodes.name: Edge-addability
nodes.statement: Another useful property of $\mathcal{P}(n)$ is \textit{edge-addability}: for each graph $G$ in $\mathcal{P}(n)$, any graph that is obtained from $G$ by adding an edge between two vertices in different components is also in $\mathcal{P}(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: A class is edge-addable if adding an edge between two components keeps the graph in the class; $\mathcal{P}(n)$ is.

nodes.name: Random planar graph with edge probability p
nodes.statement: The \textit{random planar graph with edge probability $p$} is defined to be the graph obtained by repeatedly sampling a (general) random graph with edge probability~$p$ until we find one that is planar.
nodes.definiendum: random planar graph with edge probability $p$

nodes.name: Uniform random planar graph P_n
nodes.statement: However, if we let $p=\frac{1}{2}$ then we obtain $P_{n}$, the graph taken uniformly at random from the set of all graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n)$.

nodes.name: Exponential generating function
nodes.statement: The \textit{exponential generating function} for a class $\mathcal{A}$ is defined to be $A(x) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{a_{n}}{n!} x^{n}$, where $a_{n}$ denotes the number of elements of $\mathcal{A}$ that have parameter $n$ (e.g.~$\mathcal{A}$ could be the class of planar graphs and $a_{n}$ could be $|\mathcal{P}(n)|$).

nodes.name: Random planar graph process
nodes.statement: The \textit{random planar graph process} is a random graph process equipped with an additional acceptance test: before we insert an edge, we check whether the resulting graph would be planar and, if not, we reject the edge (and never look at it again).
differentia: equipped with an additional acceptance test

nodes.name: Uniform random planar graph with m edges P_{n,m}
nodes.statement: The \textit{uniform random planar graph with $m$ edges}, $P_{n,m}$, is the graph taken uniformly at random from the set of all graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n)$ with exactly $m$ edges.
definiendum: uniform random planar graph with $m$ edges

nodes.name: Class P(n,m)
nodes.statement: We shall use $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ to denote this set.

nodes.name: Planarity of sparse uniform random graphs
nodes.statement: It is known from general uniform random graph theory (see, for example, Theorem 5.5 of \cite{jan}) that, \textit{asymptotically almost surely} (a.a.s., that is, with probability tending to $1$ as $n$ tends to infinity), a graph taken uniformly at random from the class of all size $m$ graphs on $\{1,2, \ldots, n \}$ will be planar if $\frac{m(n)}{n}$ is bounded above by $C < \frac{1}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: A.a.s. a uniform random graph with $m\le Cn$ edges, $C<1/2$, is planar (also defines a.a.s.).
conclusions: a graph taken uniformly at random from the class of all size $m$ graphs on $\{1,2, \ldots, n \}$ will be planar

nodes.name: Class P_c(n,m) of connected planar graphs
nodes.statement: Generating functions were used in \cite{gim} to give rather precise asymptotic expressions for both $|\mathcal{P}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)|$ and $|\mathcal{P}_{c}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)|$ for fixed $q \in (1,3)$, where $\mathcal{P}_{c}(n,m)$ denotes the class of connected graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$, and these results can be combined to give an expression for $\mathbf{P}\left[P_{n,\lfloor qn \rfloor} \textrm{ will be connected}\right]$ for~$q \in~\!(1,3)$.

nodes.name: Pendant edges and addable edges
nodes.statement: In Sections~\ref{pen} and \ref{add} of this thesis, we shall then do the groundwork for our later theorems by investigating the number of pendant edges (i.e.~the number of edges incident to a vertex of degree $1$) and the number of addable edges (i.e.~the number of edges that can be added individually to a planar graph without destroying planarity).

nodes.name: Asymptotic number of labelled planar graphs
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray*} |\mathcal{P}(n)| \sim g \cdot n^{-7/2} \gamma_{l}^{n}n! , \end{eqnarray*} where $g \approx 0.4260938569 \cdot 10^{-5}$ and $\gamma_{l} \approx 27.2268777685$ are constants given by explicit analytic expressions.
nodes.statement_short: $|\mathcal{P}(n)| \sim g n^{-7/2}\gamma_l^n n!$ with explicit constants $g$ and $\gamma_l\approx 27.23$.
nodes.label: gim T1

nodes.name: Sketch of proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sketch of Proof} Since a planar graph is a set of connected planar graphs, the~e.g.f.~(exponential generating function) for the class of planar graphs can be expressed in terms of the e.g.f.~for the class of connected planar graphs. Similarly, a connected planar graph may be decomposed into $2$-connected components, and so this enables us to relate the e.g.f.~for the class of connected planar graphs to the e.g.f.~for the class of $2$-connected planar graphs. This latter class has already been analysed in \cite{ben}, via a further decomposition into $3$-connected components (which have a unique embedding in the sphere~\cite{whi}) and the use of known results on planar map enumeration. Hence, we are then able to use the e.g.f.~equations (together with a large amount of algebraic manipulation) to obtain our asymptotic estimate for $|\mathcal{P}(n)|$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose planar graphs into connected, 2-connected and 3-connected parts and solve the resulting e.g.f. equations.

nodes.name: Reduce to connected and 2-connected classes
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sketch of Proof} Since a planar graph is a set of connected planar graphs, the~e.g.f.~(exponential generating function) for the class of planar graphs can be expressed in terms of the e.g.f.~for the class of connected planar graphs. Similarly, a connected planar graph may be decomposed into $2$-connected components, and so this enables us to relate the e.g.f.~for the class of connected planar graphs to the e.g.f.~for the class of $2$-connected planar graphs.
nodes.statement_short: Express the e.g.f. of planar graphs via connected, then 2-connected, planar graphs.

nodes.name: Use known analysis of 2-connected planar graphs
nodes.statement: This latter class has already been analysed in \cite{ben}, via a further decomposition into $3$-connected components (which have a unique embedding in the sphere~\cite{whi}) and the use of known results on planar map enumeration.
nodes.statement_short: The 2-connected class is known via 3-connected decomposition and map enumeration.

nodes.name: Derive the asymptotic estimate
nodes.statement: Hence, we are then able to use the e.g.f.~equations (together with a large amount of algebraic manipulation) to obtain our asymptotic estimate for $|\mathcal{P}(n)|$.
nodes.statement_short: Algebraic manipulation of the e.g.f. equations gives the estimate.

nodes.name: Growth constant of labelled planar graphs
nodes.statement: Note that Proposition~\ref{gim T1} implies that $\left(\frac{|\mathcal{P}(n)|}{n!}\right)^{1/n} \to \gamma_{l} \textrm{ as } n \to \infty$.

nodes.name: Labelled planar graph growth constant
nodes.statement: Thus, we call $\gamma_{l}$ the \textit{labelled planar graph growth constant}.

nodes.name: Poisson limit of component counts in P_n
nodes.statement: Let $H_{1},\ldots ,H_{r}$ denote a fixed collection of pairwise non-isomorphic connected planar graphs, and let $X_{n}^{(i)}$ denote a random variable which counts the number of components isomorphic to $H_{i}$ in $P_{n}$. Then $\left( X_{n}^{(1)},\ldots,X_{n}^{(r)} \right) \stackrel{d}{\to} \left( Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{r} \right)$, where $Z_{i} \in \emph{Poi} \left( \left(|\emph{Aut}(H_{i})| \gamma _{l}^{|H_{i}|}\right)^{-1} \right) $ are independent.
nodes.statement_short: Component counts of fixed graphs $H_i$ in $P_n$ converge jointly to independent Poissons with means $1/(|Aut(H_i)|\gamma_l^{|H_i|})$.
assumptions: Let $H_{1},\ldots ,H_{r}$ denote a fixed collection of pairwise non-isomorphic connected planar graphs,
let $X_{n}^{(i)}$ denote a random variable which counts the number of components isomorphic to $H_{i}$ in $P_{n}$.
nodes.label: mcd 5.6

nodes.name: Sketch of proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sketch of Proof} We construct graphs of order $n$ with at least $k_{i}$ components isomorphic to $H_{i}$, for all $i$, and find that we have built $|\mathcal{P}(n)| \mathbf{E} \left[ \prod_{i \leq r} \left( (X_{n}^{(i)})_{k_{i}} \right) \right]$ graphs in total, where $(X)_{k} = X(X-1)\cdots(X-k+1)$ denotes the $k$th factorial moment. Thus, we obtain a formula for $\mathbf{E} \left[ \prod_{i \leq r} \left( (X_{n}^{(i)})_{k_{i}} \right) \right]$, which turns out to simplify in terms of $I_{n}$, the expected number of isolated vertices in $P_{n}$. But $I_{n} = n\mathbf{P}[v_{n} \textrm{ is isolated in }P_{n}] = \frac{n|\mathcal{P}(n-1)|}{|\mathcal{P}(n)|} \to \gamma_{l}^{-1}$, by Theorem~\ref{gim T1}. A standard result on the factorial moments of the Poisson distribution then completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Method of factorial moments: count constructed graphs to compute factorial moments, which tend to Poisson ones.

nodes.name: Construct graphs with prescribed components
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sketch of Proof} We construct graphs of order $n$ with at least $k_{i}$ components isomorphic to $H_{i}$, for all $i$, and find that we have built $|\mathcal{P}(n)| \mathbf{E} \left[ \prod_{i \leq r} \left( (X_{n}^{(i)})_{k_{i}} \right) \right]$ graphs in total, where $(X)_{k} = X(X-1)\cdots(X-k+1)$ denotes the $k$th factorial moment.
nodes.statement_short: Counting constructed graphs gives $|\mathcal{P}(n)|$ times the joint factorial moment.

nodes.name: Formula for the factorial moments
nodes.statement: Thus, we obtain a formula for $\mathbf{E} \left[ \prod_{i \leq r} \left( (X_{n}^{(i)})_{k_{i}} \right) \right]$, which turns out to simplify in terms of $I_{n}$, the expected number of isolated vertices in $P_{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: The factorial moments simplify in terms of the expected number $I_n$ of isolated vertices.

nodes.name: Limit of I_n
nodes.statement: But $I_{n} = n\mathbf{P}[v_{n} \textrm{ is isolated in }P_{n}] = \frac{n|\mathcal{P}(n-1)|}{|\mathcal{P}(n)|} \to \gamma_{l}^{-1}$, by Theorem~\ref{gim T1}.

nodes.name: Poisson factorial moments
nodes.statement: A standard result on the factorial moments of the Poisson distribution then completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by the standard factorial-moment characterisation of the Poisson law.

nodes.name: Limiting probability of a component isomorphic to H in P_n
nodes.statement: As a corollary to Theorem~\ref{mcd 5.6}, we can see that the limiting probability for $P_{n}$ having a component isomorphic to $H$ is $1-e^{-\frac{1}{\left( \left| \scriptsize{\textrm{Aut}}(H) \right| \gamma_{l} ^{|H|}\right)}}$.
conclusions: the limiting probability for $P_{n}$ having a component isomorphic to $H$ is $1-e^{-\frac{1}{\left( \left| \scriptsize{\textrm{Aut}}(H) \right| \gamma_{l} ^{|H|}\right)}}$

nodes.name: Appearance
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a graph on the vertex set $\{1,2,\ldots,h\},$ and let $G$ be a graph on the vertex set $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$, where $n>h$. Let $W \subset V(G)$ with $|W|=h$, and let the `root' $r_{W}$ denote the least element in $W$. We say that $H$ \textbf{\emph{appears}} at~$W$ in $G$ if (a) the increasing bijection from ${1,\ldots,h}$ to $W$ gives an isomorphism between $H$ and the induced subgraph $G[W]$ of $G$; and (b) there is exactly one edge in $G$ between $W$ and the rest of $G$, and this edge is incident with the root $r_{W}$. We let $\mathbf{f_{H}(G)}$ denote the number of appearances of $H$ in $G$, that is the number of sets $W \subset V(G)$ such that $H$ appears at $W$ in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: $H$ appears at $W$ in $G$ if $G[W]\cong H$ order-preservingly and exactly one edge, at the root, joins $W$ to the rest; $f_H(G)$ counts appearances.
nodes.label: defapps

nodes.name: Asymptotic normality of appearances in P_n
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a fixed connected planar graph on the vertex set $\{ 1,\ldots,h \}$. Then $f_{H}(P_{n})$ is asymptotically Normal, and the mean~$\mu_{n}$ and variance $\sigma_{n}^{2}$ satisfy $\mu_{n} \sim \frac{n}{\gamma_{l}^{h}h!} \textrm{ and } \sigma_{n}^{2} \sim \frac{n}{\gamma_{l}}$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be a fixed connected planar graph on the vertex set $\{ 1,\ldots,h \}$.
conclusions: Then $f_{H}(P_{n})$ is asymptotically Normal, and the mean~$\mu_{n}$ and variance $\sigma_{n}^{2}$ satisfy $\mu_{n} \sim \frac{n}{\gamma_{l}^{h}h!} \textrm{ and } \sigma_{n}^{2} \sim \frac{n}{\gamma_{l}}$.
nodes.label: gim T4

nodes.name: Linearly many copies of H in P_n
nodes.statement: Thus, a.a.s.~$P_{n}$ will contain at least linearly many copies of any given connected planar graph.
conclusions: a.a.s.~$P_{n}$ will contain at least linearly many copies of any given connected planar graph

nodes.name: Stochastic domination of the number of components of P_n
nodes.statement: The random number $\kappa (P_{n})$ of components of $P_{n}$ is stochastically dominated \footnote{We say the distribution $(p_{j})$ is \textit{stochastically dominated} by the distribution $(q_{j})$ to mean that we have $\Sigma_{k \leq l} \phantom{p} p_{k} \phantom{p} \geq \phantom{p} \Sigma_{k \leq l} \phantom{p} q_{k} \phantom{p} \forall l$.} by $1+X$, where $X$ has the Poisson distribution with mean $1$. In particular, \begin{displaymath} \mathbf{P} [P_{n} \textrm{ connected} ] \geq 1/e \textrm{ and } \mathbf{E}[\kappa (P_{n})] \leq 2. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: $\kappa(P_n)$ is stochastically dominated by $1+\mathrm{Poi}(1)$; so $P_n$ is connected w.p. $\ge 1/e$.
conclusions: The random number $\kappa (P_{n})$ of components of $P_{n}$ is stochastically dominated
nodes.label: mcd 2.1

nodes.name: Asymptotic distribution of the number of components of P_n
nodes.statement: Asymptotically, $\kappa (P_{n}) -~\!1$ is distributed like a Poisson law of parameter $\upsilon$, where $\upsilon \approx 0.0374393660$ is a constant given by an explicit analytic expression. In particular, \begin{eqnarray*} \mathbf{P}[P_{n} \textrm{ connected}] & \to & e^{-\upsilon} \approx 0.9632528217 \\ \textrm{ and } \mathbf{E}[\kappa (P_{n})] & \to & 1+ \upsilon \approx 1.0374393660. \end{eqnarray*}
conclusions: Asymptotically, $\kappa (P_{n}) -~\!1$ is distributed like a Poisson law of parameter $\upsilon$,
nodes.label: gim T6

nodes.name: Asymptotic number of planar graphs with n vertices and qn edges
nodes.statement: Let $q \in (1,3)$. Then \begin{eqnarray*} |\mathcal{P}(n,\lfloor qn \rfloor)| & \sim & g(q) \cdot \left( u(q) \right) ^{qn - \lfloor qn \rfloor} \cdot n^{-4} \gamma (q)^{n}n! \\ \textrm{and } \phantom{w} |\mathcal{P}_{c}(n,\lfloor qn \rfloor)| & \sim & g_{c}(q) \cdot \left( u(q) \right) ^{qn - \lfloor qn \rfloor} \cdot n^{-4} \gamma (q)^{n}n!, \end{eqnarray*} where $g(q)$, $g_{c}(q)$, $u(q)$ and $\gamma (q) >0$ are computable analytic functions.
nodes.statement_short: Precise asymptotics $g(q)u(q)^{qn-\lfloor qn\rfloor}n^{-4}\gamma(q)^n n!$ for planar and connected planar graphs with $\lfloor qn\rfloor$ edges.
nodes.label: gim T3

nodes.name: Sketch of proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sketch of Proof} We define the \textit{bivariate exponential generating function} for a class of graphs, $\mathcal{A}$, to be $A(x,y) = \sum_{n,m \geq 0} \frac{a_{n,m}}{n!} x^{n}y^{m}$, where $a_{n,m}$ denotes the number of graphs in $\mathcal{A}$ that have order $n$ and size $m$. Hence, we may again use the decomposition of the proof of Proposition~\ref{gim T1} to obtain the given asymptotic estimates.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the decomposition argument of Proposition 1 with bivariate e.g.f.s.

nodes.name: Limiting connectivity probability strictly between 0 and 1
nodes.statement: Note this provides an expression for $\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbf{P}\left[P_{n,\lfloor qn \rfloor} \textrm{ will be connected}\right]$. As it turns out, this limit is strictly between $0$ and $1$ for all $q \in (1,3)$.
conclusions: this limit is strictly between $0$ and $1$ for all $q \in (1,3)$

nodes.name: Growth function for q
nodes.statement: Analogously to with $\gamma_{l}$, we call $\gamma (q)$ the \textit{growth function for $q$}.

nodes.name: Properties of the growth function gamma(q)
nodes.statement: For each $q \in [0,3]$, there is a finite constant $\gamma(q) \geq 0$ such that, as $n \to \infty$, if $0 \leq q < 3$ then both $(|\mathcal{P}_{c}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)|/n!)^{1/n}$ and $(|\mathcal{P} (n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)|/n!)^{1/n}$ tend to $\gamma(q)$, and $(|\mathcal{P}(n,3n-6)|/n!)^{1/n}$ tends to $\gamma(3)$. The function $\gamma(q)$ is equal to $0$ for $q \in [0,1)$ and is then unimodal and uniformly continuous on $[1,3]$, satisfying $\gamma(1) = e$, $\gamma(3) = 256/27$ and achieving a maximum value of $\gamma_{l}$ at $q = \mathbf{E} \left( e(P_{n}) \right) \approx 2.2132652385$. \\
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma(q)$ exists, is $0$ on $[0,1)$, unimodal and uniformly continuous on $[1,3]$, $\gamma(1)=e$, $\gamma(3)=256/27$, maximum $\gamma_l$.
nodes.origin_citation: Gerke, McDiarmid, Steger & Weissl [ger]; Gimenez & Noy [gim]
nodes.label: ger T2.1

nodes.name: Uniform convergence to the growth function
nodes.statement: Let $a \in (1,3)$ and let $\eta>0$. Then there exists $n_{0}$ such that for all $n \geq n_{0}$ and all $s \in [an,3n-6]$ we have \begin{displaymath} \left| \left( \frac{|\mathcal{P}(n,s)|}{n!} \right)^{1/n} - \gamma \left( \frac{s}{n} \right) \right| < \eta. \end{displaymath} \\
conclusions: Then there exists $n_{0}$ such that for all $n \geq n_{0}$ and all $s \in [an,3n-6]$ we have
nodes.label: ger L2.9

nodes.name: Linearly many appearances in P_{n,qn}
nodes.statement: Let $q \in [1,3)$ and let $H$ be a fixed connected planar graph on the vertices $\{1, \ldots ,h\}$, with the extra condition that $H$ is a tree if $ q=1$. Then there exists $\alpha= \alpha(H,q)>0$ such that \begin{displaymath} \mathbf{P} \left[f_{H} \left( P_{n, \lfloor qn \rfloor} \right) \leq \alpha n \right] = e^{- \Omega (n)}. \end{displaymath}
assumptions: Let $q \in [1,3)$ and let $H$ be a fixed connected planar graph on the vertices $\{1, \ldots ,h\}$, with the extra condition that $H$ is a tree if $ q=1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13
nodes.statement: In the proof of Proposition~\ref{ger T3.1} in \cite{ger}, it is actually shown that $\exists N(H,q)$ and $\alpha (H,q) >0$ such that $\mathbf{P}[f_{H}(P_{n, \lfloor qn \rfloor}) \leq \alpha n] < e^{- \alpha n} \textrm{ } \forall n \geq N.$ It will suffice to show that this holds uniformly, in the sense that $\exists N(H,b,B)$ and $\alpha(H,b,B)>0$ such that, \textit{for all $q \in [b,B]$}, we have $\mathbf{P}[f_{H}(P_{n, \lfloor qn \rfloor}) \leq \alpha n] < e^{- \alpha n} \textrm{ } \forall n \geq N$. The proof of Proposition~\ref{ger T3.1} given in \cite{ger} implicitly provides us with the value $\alpha (H,q) = \frac{1}{9e^{2}(\gamma (q))^{h+x}(h+x+2)(h+x)!}$, where $x$ is the least integer such that $\frac{x+2}{x+1} \leq~q$ and $\frac{3x-5}{x+1} > q$. Recall from Proposition~\ref{ger T2.1} that $\gamma (q) \in [e, \gamma_{l}]$~$\forall q \in [1,3]$. Thus, it follows that we may take $\alpha$, \textit{independently of $q$}, to be $\frac{1}{9e^{2}\gamma_{l}^{h+z}(h+z+2)(h+z)!}$, where $z$ is the least integer such that $\frac{z+2}{z+1} \leq b$ and $\frac{3z-5}{z+1} > B$. The value of $N(H,q)$ provided by the proof of Proposition~\ref{ger T3.1} given in \cite{ger} depends on~$q$ only in that we must have \begin{displaymath} (1-\epsilon)^{n}n!(\gamma (q))^{n} \leq |\mathcal{P}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)| \leq (1+\epsilon)^{n}n!(\gamma (q))^{n} \textrm{ }\forall n \geq N, \end{displaymath} where $\epsilon$ is defined by the equation $\left( \frac{1}{9} \right)^{\alpha} = 1-3\epsilon$. Thus, since our $\epsilon$ will only be a function of $H,b$ and $B$, it suffices for us to prove $\exists N(b,B,\epsilon)$ such that, \emph{for all} $q \in [b,B]$, we have \begin{displaymath} (1-\epsilon)^{n}n!(\gamma (q))^{n} \leq |\mathcal{P}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)| \leq (1+ \epsilon)^{n}n!(\gamma (q))^{n} \textrm{ }\forall n \geq N. \end{displaymath} By uniform convergence (Proposition~\ref{ger L2.9}), we know that $\exists N_{1} (b, \epsilon)$ such that, for all $q \in [b,3)$, we have $\left|\left(\frac{|\mathcal{P}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)|}{n!} \right)^{1/n} - \gamma \left(\frac{\lfloor qn \rfloor}{n} \right)\right| < \frac{\epsilon e}{2} $ $\forall n \geq N_{1}$. But since $\gamma (q)$ is uniformly continuous on $[1,3]$ (Proposition~\ref{ger T2.1}), we also know $\exists N_{2} (\epsilon)$ such that, for all $q \in [1,3]$, we have $\left|\gamma \left(\frac{\lfloor qn \rfloor}{n} \right)- \gamma (q)\right| < \frac{\epsilon e}{2} $ $\forall n \geq N_{2}$. Thus, for all $q \in [b,3)$, we have \begin{displaymath} \left|\left(\frac{|\mathcal{P}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)|}{n!} \right)^{1/n} - \gamma (q)\right| < \epsilon e \leq \epsilon \gamma (q) \textrm{ } \forall n \geq N(b,B, \epsilon) = \max \{ N_{1}, N_{2} \}. \end{displaymath} Hence, we are done. $\phantom{qwerty}$ \setlength{\unitlength}{.25cm} \begin{picture}(1,1) \put(0,0){\line(1,0){1}} \put(0,0){\line(0,1){1}} \put(1,1){\line(-1,0){1}} \put(1,1){\line(0,-1){1}} \end{picture} \\ \\ The first part of our pendant edges/vertices of degree $1$ result now follows:
nodes.statement_short: Make the constants in the proof of Proposition 10 uniform in $q\in[b,B]$ using uniform convergence and continuity of $\gamma$.

nodes.name: Recall the bound from [ger]
nodes.statement: In the proof of Proposition~\ref{ger T3.1} in \cite{ger}, it is actually shown that $\exists N(H,q)$ and $\alpha (H,q) >0$ such that $\mathbf{P}[f_{H}(P_{n, \lfloor qn \rfloor}) \leq \alpha n] < e^{- \alpha n} \textrm{ } \forall n \geq N.$

nodes.name: Reduce to uniformity in q
nodes.statement: It will suffice to show that this holds uniformly, in the sense that $\exists N(H,b,B)$ and $\alpha(H,b,B)>0$ such that, \textit{for all $q \in [b,B]$}, we have $\mathbf{P}[f_{H}(P_{n, \lfloor qn \rfloor}) \leq \alpha n] < e^{- \alpha n} \textrm{ } \forall n \geq N$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to make $N$ and $\alpha$ independent of $q\in[b,B]$.

nodes.name: Explicit value of alpha(H,q)
nodes.statement: The proof of Proposition~\ref{ger T3.1} given in \cite{ger} implicitly provides us with the value $\alpha (H,q) = \frac{1}{9e^{2}(\gamma (q))^{h+x}(h+x+2)(h+x)!}$, where $x$ is the least integer such that $\frac{x+2}{x+1} \leq~q$ and $\frac{3x-5}{x+1} > q$.
nodes.statement_short: The proof in [ger] gives an explicit $\alpha(H,q)$.

nodes.name: Range of gamma(q)
nodes.statement: Recall from Proposition~\ref{ger T2.1} that $\gamma (q) \in [e, \gamma_{l}]$~$\forall q \in [1,3]$.

nodes.name: Choose alpha independent of q
nodes.statement: Thus, it follows that we may take $\alpha$, \textit{independently of $q$}, to be $\frac{1}{9e^{2}\gamma_{l}^{h+z}(h+z+2)(h+z)!}$, where $z$ is the least integer such that $\frac{z+2}{z+1} \leq b$ and $\frac{3z-5}{z+1} > B$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\alpha$ can be chosen independently of $q$.

nodes.name: Reduce N to uniform counting bounds
nodes.statement: The value of $N(H,q)$ provided by the proof of Proposition~\ref{ger T3.1} given in \cite{ger} depends on~$q$ only in that we must have \begin{displaymath} (1-\epsilon)^{n}n!(\gamma (q))^{n} \leq |\mathcal{P}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)| \leq (1+\epsilon)^{n}n!(\gamma (q))^{n} \textrm{ }\forall n \geq N, \end{displaymath} where $\epsilon$ is defined by the equation $\left( \frac{1}{9} \right)^{\alpha} = 1-3\epsilon$. Thus, since our $\epsilon$ will only be a function of $H,b$ and $B$, it suffices for us to prove $\exists N(b,B,\epsilon)$ such that, \emph{for all} $q \in [b,B]$, we have \begin{displaymath} (1-\epsilon)^{n}n!(\gamma (q))^{n} \leq |\mathcal{P}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)| \leq (1+ \epsilon)^{n}n!(\gamma (q))^{n} \textrm{ }\forall n \geq N. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to have the counting estimate for $|\mathcal{P}(n,\lfloor qn\rfloor)|$ uniformly in $q$.

nodes.name: Apply uniform convergence
nodes.statement: By uniform convergence (Proposition~\ref{ger L2.9}), we know that $\exists N_{1} (b, \epsilon)$ such that, for all $q \in [b,3)$, we have $\left|\left(\frac{|\mathcal{P}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)|}{n!} \right)^{1/n} - \gamma \left(\frac{\lfloor qn \rfloor}{n} \right)\right| < \frac{\epsilon e}{2} $ $\forall n \geq N_{1}$.

nodes.name: Apply uniform continuity
nodes.statement: But since $\gamma (q)$ is uniformly continuous on $[1,3]$ (Proposition~\ref{ger T2.1}), we also know $\exists N_{2} (\epsilon)$ such that, for all $q \in [1,3]$, we have $\left|\gamma \left(\frac{\lfloor qn \rfloor}{n} \right)- \gamma (q)\right| < \frac{\epsilon e}{2} $ $\forall n \geq N_{2}$.

nodes.name: Combine to finish
nodes.statement: Thus, for all $q \in [b,3)$, we have \begin{displaymath} \left|\left(\frac{|\mathcal{P}(n, \lfloor qn \rfloor)|}{n!} \right)^{1/n} - \gamma (q)\right| < \epsilon e \leq \epsilon \gamma (q) \textrm{ } \forall n \geq N(b,B, \epsilon) = \max \{ N_{1}, N_{2} \}. \end{displaymath} Hence, we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Combine $N_1,N_2$ to get the uniform estimate.

Then there exist constants $N(b,B)$ and $\beta(b,B) >0$ such that \begin{displaymath} \mathbf{P}[P_{n,m} \textrm{ will have $< \beta n$ vertices of degree }1] < e^{- \beta n} \textrm{ } \forall n \geq N. \end{displaymath}

nodes.name: Sketch of proof of Lemma 15
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sketch of Proof} We suppose, hoping for a contradiction, that there will be a decent proportion of graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with only `a few' vertices of degree~$1$ and we consider separately the cases when (a)~there are also `many' isolated vertices and (b) there are not `many' isolated vertices. For case (a), we construct new graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ by turning some of the isolated vertices into vertices of degree~$1$ (and deleting some edges elsewhere) and find that we can construct so many graphs that we obtain our desired contradiction. For case (b), we note that we must have `lots' of vertices of degree $2$. In fact, we must have `lots' of vertices of degree $2$ that are adjacent only to other vertices of degree $2$. Such a vertex must belong either to a component that is a triangle or to a larger component. In both cases, we construct new graphs by turning the chosen vertex into a vertex of degree $1$ (and inserting an edge elsewhere). Again, we find that we can construct so many graphs that we obtain our desired contradiction. In all cases of the proof, the key idea is to construct our graphs in such a way that there is not much double-counting. This is helped by our assumption that we started with only `a few' vertices of degree $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction by counting: build many graphs with more degree-1 vertices, in two cases on the number of isolated vertices.

nodes.name: Assume few degree-1 vertices
nodes.statement: \textbf{Sketch of Proof} We suppose, hoping for a contradiction, that there will be a decent proportion of graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with only `a few' vertices of degree~$1$ and we consider separately the cases when (a)~there are also `many' isolated vertices and (b) there are not `many' isolated vertices.
nodes.statement_short: Assume many graphs have few degree-1 vertices; split on many/few isolated vertices.

nodes.name: Case (a): many isolated vertices
nodes.statement: For case (a), we construct new graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ by turning some of the isolated vertices into vertices of degree~$1$ (and deleting some edges elsewhere) and find that we can construct so many graphs that we obtain our desired contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Turn isolated vertices into degree-1 vertices, deleting edges elsewhere.

nodes.name: Case (b): few isolated vertices
nodes.statement: For case (b), we note that we must have `lots' of vertices of degree $2$. In fact, we must have `lots' of vertices of degree $2$ that are adjacent only to other vertices of degree $2$. Such a vertex must belong either to a component that is a triangle or to a larger component. In both cases, we construct new graphs by turning the chosen vertex into a vertex of degree $1$ (and inserting an edge elsewhere). Again, we find that we can construct so many graphs that we obtain our desired contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Use many degree-2 vertices adjacent only to degree-2 vertices to create degree-1 vertices.

nodes.name: Control double counting
nodes.statement: In all cases of the proof, the key idea is to construct our graphs in such a way that there is not much double-counting. This is helped by our assumption that we started with only `a few' vertices of degree $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Little double counting, thanks to few initial degree-1 vertices.

onumber \ & < & 2 \epsilon n +  eta n + 2\delta n \end{eqnarray} and so  egin{eqnarray*} d_{2} & = & n - \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} - d_{1} - d_{0} \ & > & n - 2 \epsilon n -  eta n - 2 \delta n -  eta n - \epsilon n \ & = & \left( 1-3\epsilon - 2 eta -2\delta ight)n. \end{eqnarray*} We shall now see that, in fact, $G$ must contain many vertices of degree~$2$ that are adjacent only to other vertices of degree $2$. Recall from (ef{eq:label1}) that we have $\sum_{i \geq 1}id_{i} \leq 2d_{0} + 2d_{1} + 2d_{2} + 2 \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} +~2\delta n$. Thus,  egin{eqnarray*} \sum_{i \geq 3}id_{i} & \leq & 2d_{0} + d_{1} + 2\sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} + 2\delta n \ & < & 2 \epsilon n +  eta n + 2(2 \epsilon n +  eta n + 2\delta n) + 2 \delta n \phantom{www} 	extrm{ by (ef{eq:label2})} \ & = & (6 \epsilon + 3  eta + 6 \delta)n. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, at most $(6 \epsilon + 3  eta + 6 \delta)n$ of the degree $2$ vertices will be adjacent to a vertex of degree $\geq 3$. Similarly, at most $d_{1} <  eta n$ of the degree $2$ vertices will be adjacent to a vertex of degree $1$. Hence, at least $d_{2} -  eta n - (6 \epsilon +3  eta + 6 \delta)n > (1- 3 \epsilon - 2  eta - 2 \delta)n -  eta n - (6 \epsilon + 3  eta + 6 \delta)n = (1-9 \epsilon - 6  eta - 8\delta)n$ of the degree~$2$ vertices will be adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices. Let $A$ denote the set of vertices of degree $2$ that are adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices. Using $G$, we shall construct a graph (in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$) with $ \geq  eta n$ vertices of degree $1$ by the following algorithm: \ \ Stage $1$: \ Let $B_{0} = \emptyset$ and let $i=1$. \ \ Stage $2$: \ Choose a vertex, $v_{i}$, in $A-B_{i-1}$ (it will become clear that $v_{i}$ will still be a degree $2$ vertex that is adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices). Let the vertices adjacent to $v_{i}$ be denoted by $u_{i}$ and $w_{i}$. \ \ Stage $3a$ (If $u_{i}w_{i}$ $\in E(G)$): \ If $u_{i}w_{i}$ is an edge in $G$ (in which case $\{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i} \}$ form a component that is a triangle, since $d(u_{i}) = d(v_{i}) = d(w_{i}) =2$), then delete the edge $v_{i}w_{i}$ and join $w_{i}$ to a vertex $x_{i} 
otin (B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i} \} )$ (see Figure~ef{fig3a}). This is possible if $i \leq \lceil  eta n ceil$, since it will become clear that $|B_{i-1}| + 2 \leq 6(i-1) +2 <6( \lceil  eta n ceil -1) +2 < n$ if $ eta <  rac{1}{6}$. Planarity will be maintained, since $w_{i}$ and $x_{i}$ were in separate components. If $d(x_{i}) 
eq 2$, let $B_{i} = B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i} \}$. If $d(x_{i}) = 2$, let the vertices adjacent to $x_{i}$ be denoted by $y_{i}$ and $z_{i}$ and let $B_{i} = B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i}, x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i} \}$. Thus, as already mentioned, it is clear that $|B_{i}|$ increases by at most $6$ in each iteration and that $A-B_{i}$ still just contains degree $2$ vertices that are adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices.  egin{figure} [ht] \setlength{\unitlength}{1cm}  egin{picture}(20,0.5)(0,0.25) \put(3.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(3.5,1){\line(1,-2){0.5}} \put(3.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.65,0.9){$v_{i}$} \put(3,0){\line(1,0){1}} \put(3,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(4,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(2.7,-0.3){$u_{i}$} \put(3.7,-0.3){$w_{i}$} \put(5,0.5){\vector(1,0){1}} \put(7.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(7.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(7.65,0.9){$v_{i}$} \put(7,0){\line(1,0){1.5}} \put(7,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.5,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(6.7,-0.3){$u_{i}$} \put(7.7,-0.3){$w_{i}$} \put(8.3,-0.3){$x_{i}$} \put(8.5,0){\line(1,0){0.2}} \put(8.8,0){\line(1,0){0.2}} \put(8.5,0){\line(2,1){0.4}} \put(8.5,0){\line(2,-1){0.4}} \end{picture} \caption{Constructing a vertex of degree $1$ in Stage $3a$.} \end{figure} \ Stage $3b$ (If $u_{i}w_{i}$ $
otin E(G)$): \ If $u_{i}w_{i}$ is not an edge in $G$, then insert an edge between $u_{i}$ and $w_{i}$ (this can be done arbitrarily close to the edges $u_{i}v_{i}$ and $v_{i}w_{i}$, so planarity is maintained). Delete the edge $v_{i}w_{i}$. Let $x_{i}$ denote the neighbour of $u_{i}$ that is not $v_{i}$ or $w_{i}$ and let $B_{i} = B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i}, x_{i} \}$.  egin{figure} [ht] \setlength{\unitlength}{1cm}  egin{picture}(20,2.75)(0,0.5) \put(4,3){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(4,3){\line(1,-2){0.5}} \put(3.5,2){\line(0,-1){1}} \put(4,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.9,3.2){$v_{i}$} \put(3.5,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.1,2){$u_{i}$} \put(4.5,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(4.6,2){$w_{i}$} \put(3.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.1,1){$x_{i}$} \put(3.5,1){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(3.5,0.5){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(3.5,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.8,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.2,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(5.5,1.5){\vector(1,0){1}} \put(8.5,3){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(8,2){\line(0,-1){1}} \put(8,2){\line(1,0){1}} \put(8.5,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.4,3.2){$v_{i}$} \put(8,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(7.6,2){$u_{i}$} \put(9,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(9.1,2){$w_{i}$} \put(8,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(7.6,1){$x_{i}$} \put(8,1){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8,0.5){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8.3,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(7.7,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \end{picture} \caption{Constructing a vertex of degree $1$ in Stage $3b$.} \end{figure} \ Stage $4$: \ If $i = \lceil  eta n ceil$, then we terminate the algorithm. Otherwise, we increase $i$ by $1$ and return to Stage $2$. \ Note that we have $d(v_{i}) = 1$ $ orall i$ in our new graph. At each iteration, we had $|A-B_{i-1}| \geq (1 - 9 \epsilon - 6  eta - 8 \delta)n - 6  eta n =(1- 9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta)n$ choices for $v_{i}$. Thus, by considering all possible initial graphs $G \in \mathcal{J}_{n}$, we have at least $(1- 9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta)^{\lceil  eta n ceil} n^{\lceil  eta n ceil}  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$ ways to construct a graph with $\geq  eta n$ vertices of degree $1$, and so it remains only to consider the amount of double-counting. Each new graph will contain at most $3 \lceil  eta n ceil$ vertices of degree $1$ (since there were $< \lceil  eta n ceil$ to begin with; we have deliberately created $\lceil  eta n ceil$; and we may have created at most one extra one each time we used Stage $3a$, if $x_{i}$ was an isolated vertex). Thus, we have $\leq 3 \lceil  eta n ceil$ possibilities for which vertex was $v_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$, which will now be adjacent only to $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$. If $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ now has degree $2$, then we must have used Stage $3a$ in the final iteration and hence $w_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ is the other neighbour of $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ and $x_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ is the remaining neighbour of $w_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$. Thus, we know how the graph changed during the final iteration. If $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ now has degree $3$, then we must have used Stage $3b$ in the final iteration and hence we have two possibilities for which vertex was $w_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ (since it must be one of the other neighbours of $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ in the new graph). Thus, we have two possibilities for how the graph changed during the final iteration. Therefore, we have at most $6 \lceil  eta n ceil$ possibilities in total for which vertex was $v_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ and how the graph looked before the final iteration. Repeating this argument, we find that we have at most $\left( 6 \lceil  eta n ceil ight)^{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ possibilities for what the original graph was and which vertices were $v_{1},v_{2}, \ldots, v_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ (in order). Hence, we have built each of our new graphs at most $(6 \lceil  eta n ceil)^{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ times and, therefore, the number of graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with $\geq  eta n$ vertices of degree $1$ is at least $ \left (  rac{(1-9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta)n}{6 \lceil  eta n ceil} ight) ^{\lceil  eta n ceil}  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$. Recall that $\delta < 1/8$. Thus, since we were free to choose $\epsilon$ and $ eta$ arbitrarily small, we may assume that $ \left (  rac{1-9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta}{6  eta} ight) >3$. Therefore, for sufficiently large~$n$, we have $ \left (  rac{(1-9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta)n}{6 \lceil  eta n ceil} ight) ^{\lceil  eta n ceil}  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| > 3^{\lceil  eta n ceil}  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| > |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$, which provides us with a contradiction. \ Thus, we get a contradiction whether $ rac{|\mathcal{H}_{n}|}{|\mathcal{P}(n,m)|} \geq  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2}$ or $ rac{|\mathcal{J}_{n}|}{|\mathcal{P}(n,m)|} \geq  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction by double counting: from graphs with few degree-1 vertices build more than $|\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$ graphs with many. Case (b) uses that most vertices have degree 2 and neighbours of degree 2.

nodes.name: Assume the bound fails
nodes.statement: \textbf{Full Proof} Choose $\beta >0$ and suppose $\exists$ arbitrarily large $n$ such that \begin{displaymath} \mathbf{P}[P_{n,m} \textrm{ will have $< \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$}] \geq e^{-\beta n}. \end{displaymath} Consider one of these $n$ and let $\mathcal{G}_{n}$ denote the set of graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with $< \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$. Thus, $|\mathcal{G}_{n}| \geq e^{-\beta n} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$. Choose $\epsilon >0$, let $\mathcal{H}_{n}$ denote the set of graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with $< \beta n$ vertices of degree~$1$ and with $> \epsilon n$ vertices of degree $0$, and let $\mathcal{J}_{n}$ denote the set of graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with $< \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$ and with $\leq \epsilon n$ vertices of degree $0$. Then $|\mathcal{H}_{n}| + |\mathcal{J}_{n}| = |\mathcal{G}_{n}| \geq e^{-\beta n} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$. Thus, either $|\mathcal{H}_{n}| \geq \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$ or $|\mathcal{J}_{n}| \geq \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume many graphs have $<\beta n$ degree-1 vertices; split them into $\mathcal{H}_n$ (many isolated vertices) and $\mathcal{J}_n$.

nodes.name: Order of choosing constants
nodes.statement: In a moment, we shall split our proof into two cases based on the observation of the previous sentence. First, though, we should just note that there will be several places later where we shall require that our choices of $\beta$, $\epsilon$ and~$n$ satisfy various inequalities. Formally, this can be done by assuming that we first chose~$\epsilon$ to be `sufficiently' small (depending on $c$ and $\delta$), that we then chose $\beta$ to be `sufficiently' small (depending on $c$, $\delta$ and $\epsilon$), and that we finally chose $n$ to be `sufficiently' large (depending on $c$, $\delta$, $\epsilon$ and $\beta$).

nodes.name: Case (a): many isolated vertices
nodes.statement: \underline{Case(a)} \\ Suppose $|\mathcal{H}_{n}| \geq \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$ and consider a graph $G \in \mathcal{H}_{n}$. Using $G$, we shall construct a graph (in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$) with $\geq \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$ as follows: \\ \\ Stage $1$: \\ Choose $\lceil \beta n \rceil$ isolated vertices (we have $\left(^{\phantom{p}d_{0}}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) > \left(^{\phantom{p}\epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right)$ choices \footnote{We use the definition $\left(^{\phantom{p}\epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) := \frac{\epsilon n \cdot (\epsilon n -1) \cdots (\epsilon n - \lceil \beta n \rceil + 1)} {\lceil \beta n \rceil !}$ if $\epsilon n$ is non-integral, as is standard.} for these, where $d_{0}$ denotes the number of vertices of degree $0$). Let us denote the chosen vertices, in order of their labels, as $v_{1}, v_{2}, \ldots, v_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$, and let $i=1$. \\ \\ Stage $2$: \\ Choose a vertex $u_{i}$ that was non-isolated in $G$ and that was also not incident to any of the edges $e_{1},e_{2}, \ldots, e_{i-1}$ defined in previous iterations (we have at least $n-d_{0}-2(i-1)$ choices, and we may assume that $\beta>0$ is sufficiently small that this is positive $\forall i \leq \lceil \beta n \rceil$, since by planarity $n-d_{0} > \frac{m}{3} \geq \frac{cn}{3}$); delete an edge $e_{i}$ incident to $u_{i}$; and join $u_{i}$ to $v_{i}$ (see Figure~\ref{penfig}). \begin{figure} [ht] \setlength{\unitlength}{1cm} \begin{picture}(10,2.5)(0,0.5) \put(4,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(4.1,3){$v_{i}$} \put(4,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.25,1.5){$e_{i}$} \put(4,2){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(4,2){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(4,1.4){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(4,2){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(4.3,1.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.5,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.8,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.2,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(4.1,2){$u_{i}$} \put(5.5,2){\vector(1,0){1}} \put(8.5,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.6,3){$v_{i}$} \put(8.5,3){\line(0,-1){1}} \put(8.5,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.5,2){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8.5,1.4){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8.5,2){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8.8,1.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8.3,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(7.7,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(8.6,2){$u_{i}$} \end{picture} \caption{Constructing a vertex of degree $1$ in Stage $2$.} \end{figure} \\ Stage $3$: \\ If $i = \lceil \beta n \rceil$, then we terminate the algorithm. Otherwise, we increase $i$ by $1$ and return to Stage $2$. \\ \\ By considering all possible initial graphs $G \in \mathcal{H}_{n}$, it is clear to see that the number of ways to build a graph with $\geq \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$ is at least $\textrm{\small{$ \left(^{\phantom{p}\epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) \left( \prod_{i=1}^{\lceil \beta n \rceil -1} (n-d_{0}-2(i-1)) \right) |\mathcal{H}_{n}| \geq \left(^{\phantom{p}\epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) \left( \frac{m}{3}-2\lceil \beta n \rceil \right)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2}|\mathcal{P}(n,m)| .$}}$ We will now consider the amount of double-counting, i.e.~how many times each new graph will be constructed. We know that each new graph will contain at most $3 \lceil \beta n \rceil$ vertices of degree $1$ (since there were $< \beta n$ to begin with; we have deliberately added $\lceil \beta n \rceil$; and we may have created at most one extra one each time we deleted an edge), so we will have at most $\left(^{3 \lceil \beta n \rceil} _{\phantom{l} \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right)$ possibilities for which were our chosen (originally isolated) vertices $v_{1},v_{2}, \ldots, v_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$. We will then have $<(n- \lceil \beta n \rceil)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ possibilities for where the edges attached to these vertices were originally. Thus, we will build each graph at most $\left(^{3 \lceil \beta n \rceil} _{\phantom{l} \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right) (n-\lceil \beta n \rceil)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ times. Therefore, the number of distinct graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with $\geq \beta n$ vertices of degree~$1$ is at least \begin{eqnarray*} & & \frac{ \left(^{\phantom{p} \epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) \left( \frac{m}{3}-2\lceil \beta n \rceil \right)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|} {\left(^{3 \lceil \beta n \rceil} _{\phantom{l} \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right) (n- \lceil \beta n \rceil)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} } \\ & \geq & \left( \frac{\epsilon n}{3 \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right) ^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \left( \frac{ \frac{m}{3}-2\lceil \beta n \rceil} {n- \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| \\ & & \textrm{ since } \frac{ \left(^{x}_{y}\right) }{ \left(^{z}_{y}\right) } = \frac{x(x-1) \cdots (x-y+1)}{z(z-1) \cdots (z-y+1)} \geq \left( \frac{x}{z} \right)^{y} \textrm{ if } z \leq x \\ & & \textrm{ and here we may assume } 3 \lceil \beta n \rceil \leq \epsilon n \\ & > & \left( \left( \frac{\epsilon}{4 \beta} \right) \left( \frac{\frac{c}{3}-3 \beta}{1-\beta} \right) \right) ^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{- \beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| \phantom{www} \textrm{ for sufficiently large $n$} \\ & > & 3^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{- \beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| \phantom{www} \textrm{ for sufficiently small $\beta$}, \\ & & \textrm{ since } \left( \frac{\epsilon}{4\beta} \right) \left( \frac{\frac{c}{3}-3\beta}{1-\beta} \right) \to \infty \textrm{ as } \beta \to 0 \\ & > & |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| \phantom{www} \textrm{ for sufficiently large $n$ (since $3>e$),} \end{eqnarray*} which is a contradiction.

nodes.name: Start from G in H_n
nodes.statement: Suppose $|\mathcal{H}_{n}| \geq \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$ and consider a graph $G \in \mathcal{H}_{n}$. Using $G$, we shall construct a graph (in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$) with $\geq \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$ as follows:
nodes.statement_short: Take $G\in\mathcal{H}_n$ and construct a new graph as follows.

nodes.name: Stage 1: choose isolated vertices
nodes.statement: Stage $1$: \\ Choose $\lceil \beta n \rceil$ isolated vertices (we have $\left(^{\phantom{p}d_{0}}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) > \left(^{\phantom{p}\epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right)$ choices \footnote{We use the definition $\left(^{\phantom{p}\epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) := \frac{\epsilon n \cdot (\epsilon n -1) \cdots (\epsilon n - \lceil \beta n \rceil + 1)} {\lceil \beta n \rceil !}$ if $\epsilon n$ is non-integral, as is standard.} for these, where $d_{0}$ denotes the number of vertices of degree $0$). Let us denote the chosen vertices, in order of their labels, as $v_{1}, v_{2}, \ldots, v_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$, and let $i=1$.

nodes.name: Stage 2: move an edge to v_i
nodes.statement: Stage $2$: \\ Choose a vertex $u_{i}$ that was non-isolated in $G$ and that was also not incident to any of the edges $e_{1},e_{2}, \ldots, e_{i-1}$ defined in previous iterations (we have at least $n-d_{0}-2(i-1)$ choices, and we may assume that $\beta>0$ is sufficiently small that this is positive $\forall i \leq \lceil \beta n \rceil$, since by planarity $n-d_{0} > \frac{m}{3} \geq \frac{cn}{3}$); delete an edge $e_{i}$ incident to $u_{i}$; and join $u_{i}$ to $v_{i}$ (see Figure~\ref{penfig}). \begin{figure} [ht] \setlength{\unitlength}{1cm} \begin{picture}(10,2.5)(0,0.5) \put(4,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(4.1,3){$v_{i}$} \put(4,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.25,1.5){$e_{i}$} \put(4,2){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(4,2){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(4,1.4){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(4,2){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(4.3,1.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.5,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.8,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.2,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(4.1,2){$u_{i}$} \put(5.5,2){\vector(1,0){1}} \put(8.5,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.6,3){$v_{i}$} \put(8.5,3){\line(0,-1){1}} \put(8.5,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.5,2){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8.5,1.4){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8.5,2){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8.8,1.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8.3,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(7.7,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(8.6,2){$u_{i}$} \end{picture} \caption{Constructing a vertex of degree $1$ in Stage $2$.} \end{figure}
nodes.statement_short: Delete an edge at a non-isolated $u_i$ and join $u_i$ to $v_i$.

nodes.name: Stage 3: iterate
nodes.statement: Stage $3$: \\ If $i = \lceil \beta n \rceil$, then we terminate the algorithm. Otherwise, we increase $i$ by $1$ and return to Stage $2$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat until $\lceil\beta n\rceil$ vertices are done.

nodes.name: Count constructions
nodes.statement: By considering all possible initial graphs $G \in \mathcal{H}_{n}$, it is clear to see that the number of ways to build a graph with $\geq \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$ is at least $\textrm{\small{$ \left(^{\phantom{p}\epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) \left( \prod_{i=1}^{\lceil \beta n \rceil -1} (n-d_{0}-2(i-1)) \right) |\mathcal{H}_{n}| \geq \left(^{\phantom{p}\epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) \left( \frac{m}{3}-2\lceil \beta n \rceil \right)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2}|\mathcal{P}(n,m)| .$}}$

nodes.name: Bound double counting
nodes.statement: We will now consider the amount of double-counting, i.e.~how many times each new graph will be constructed. We know that each new graph will contain at most $3 \lceil \beta n \rceil$ vertices of degree $1$ (since there were $< \beta n$ to begin with; we have deliberately added $\lceil \beta n \rceil$; and we may have created at most one extra one each time we deleted an edge), so we will have at most $\left(^{3 \lceil \beta n \rceil} _{\phantom{l} \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right)$ possibilities for which were our chosen (originally isolated) vertices $v_{1},v_{2}, \ldots, v_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$. We will then have $<(n- \lceil \beta n \rceil)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ possibilities for where the edges attached to these vertices were originally. Thus, we will build each graph at most $\left(^{3 \lceil \beta n \rceil} _{\phantom{l} \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right) (n-\lceil \beta n \rceil)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ times.
nodes.statement_short: Each graph is built at most $\binom{3\lceil\beta n\rceil}{\lceil\beta n\rceil}(n-\lceil\beta n\rceil)^{\lceil\beta n\rceil}$ times.

nodes.name: Contradiction in case (a)
nodes.statement: Therefore, the number of distinct graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with $\geq \beta n$ vertices of degree~$1$ is at least \begin{eqnarray*} & & \frac{ \left(^{\phantom{p} \epsilon n}_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}\right) \left( \frac{m}{3}-2\lceil \beta n \rceil \right)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|} {\left(^{3 \lceil \beta n \rceil} _{\phantom{l} \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right) (n- \lceil \beta n \rceil)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} } \\ & \geq & \left( \frac{\epsilon n}{3 \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right) ^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \left( \frac{ \frac{m}{3}-2\lceil \beta n \rceil} {n- \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| \\ & & \textrm{ since } \frac{ \left(^{x}_{y}\right) }{ \left(^{z}_{y}\right) } = \frac{x(x-1) \cdots (x-y+1)}{z(z-1) \cdots (z-y+1)} \geq \left( \frac{x}{z} \right)^{y} \textrm{ if } z \leq x \\ & & \textrm{ and here we may assume } 3 \lceil \beta n \rceil \leq \epsilon n \\ & > & \left( \left( \frac{\epsilon}{4 \beta} \right) \left( \frac{\frac{c}{3}-3 \beta}{1-\beta} \right) \right) ^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{- \beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| \phantom{www} \textrm{ for sufficiently large $n$} \\ & > & 3^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{- \beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| \phantom{www} \textrm{ for sufficiently small $\beta$}, \\ & & \textrm{ since } \left( \frac{\epsilon}{4\beta} \right) \left( \frac{\frac{c}{3}-3\beta}{1-\beta} \right) \to \infty \textrm{ as } \beta \to 0 \\ & > & |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| \phantom{www} \textrm{ for sufficiently large $n$ (since $3>e$),} \end{eqnarray*} which is a contradiction.

nodes.name: Case (b): few isolated vertices
nodes.statement:
\underline{Case(b)} \ Suppose instead that $|\mathcal{J}_{n}| \geq  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$ and consider a graph $G \in \mathcal{J}_{n}$. We shall start by showing the intuitive fact that $G$ must contain many vertices of degree $2$. Let $d_{i}$ denote the number of vertices of degree $i$ in $G$. Then  egin{eqnarray} d_{1} + 2d_{2} + 3 \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} & \leq & \sum_{i \geq 1}id_{i} 
onumber \ & = & 2m 
onumber \ & \leq & 2n +2\delta n 
onumber \ & = & 2d_{0} + 2d_{1} + 2d_{2} + 2 \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} + 2\delta n. \end{eqnarray} Thus,  egin{eqnarray} \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} & \leq & 2d_{0} + d_{1} + 2\delta n 
onumber \ & < & 2 \epsilon n +  eta n + 2\delta n \end{eqnarray} and so  egin{eqnarray*} d_{2} & = & n - \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} - d_{1} - d_{0} \ & > & n - 2 \epsilon n -  eta n - 2 \delta n -  eta n - \epsilon n \ & = & \left( 1-3\epsilon - 2 eta -2\delta ight)n. \end{eqnarray*} We shall now see that, in fact, $G$ must contain many vertices of degree~$2$ that are adjacent only to other vertices of degree $2$. Recall from (ef{eq:label1}) that we have $\sum_{i \geq 1}id_{i} \leq 2d_{0} + 2d_{1} + 2d_{2} + 2 \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} +~2\delta n$. Thus,  egin{eqnarray*} \sum_{i \geq 3}id_{i} & \leq & 2d_{0} + d_{1} + 2\sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} + 2\delta n \ & < & 2 \epsilon n +  eta n + 2(2 \epsilon n +  eta n + 2\delta n) + 2 \delta n \phantom{www} 	extrm{ by (ef{eq:label2})} \ & = & (6 \epsilon + 3  eta + 6 \delta)n. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, at most $(6 \epsilon + 3  eta + 6 \delta)n$ of the degree $2$ vertices will be adjacent to a vertex of degree $\geq 3$. Similarly, at most $d_{1} <  eta n$ of the degree $2$ vertices will be adjacent to a vertex of degree $1$. Hence, at least $d_{2} -  eta n - (6 \epsilon +3  eta + 6 \delta)n > (1- 3 \epsilon - 2  eta - 2 \delta)n -  eta n - (6 \epsilon + 3  eta + 6 \delta)n = (1-9 \epsilon - 6  eta - 8\delta)n$ of the degree~$2$ vertices will be adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices. Let $A$ denote the set of vertices of degree $2$ that are adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices. Using $G$, we shall construct a graph (in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$) with $ \geq  eta n$ vertices of degree $1$ by the following algorithm: \ \ Stage $1$: \ Let $B_{0} = \emptyset$ and let $i=1$. \ \ Stage $2$: \ Choose a vertex, $v_{i}$, in $A-B_{i-1}$ (it will become clear that $v_{i}$ will still be a degree $2$ vertex that is adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices). Let the vertices adjacent to $v_{i}$ be denoted by $u_{i}$ and $w_{i}$. \ \ Stage $3a$ (If $u_{i}w_{i}$ $\in E(G)$): \ If $u_{i}w_{i}$ is an edge in $G$ (in which case $\{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i} \}$ form a component that is a triangle, since $d(u_{i}) = d(v_{i}) = d(w_{i}) =2$), then delete the edge $v_{i}w_{i}$ and join $w_{i}$ to a vertex $x_{i} 
otin (B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i} \} )$ (see Figure~ef{fig3a}). This is possible if $i \leq \lceil  eta n ceil$, since it will become clear that $|B_{i-1}| + 2 \leq 6(i-1) +2 <6( \lceil  eta n ceil -1) +2 < n$ if $ eta <  rac{1}{6}$. Planarity will be maintained, since $w_{i}$ and $x_{i}$ were in separate components. If $d(x_{i}) 
eq 2$, let $B_{i} = B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i} \}$. If $d(x_{i}) = 2$, let the vertices adjacent to $x_{i}$ be denoted by $y_{i}$ and $z_{i}$ and let $B_{i} = B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i}, x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i} \}$. Thus, as already mentioned, it is clear that $|B_{i}|$ increases by at most $6$ in each iteration and that $A-B_{i}$ still just contains degree $2$ vertices that are adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices.  egin{figure} [ht] \setlength{\unitlength}{1cm}  egin{picture}(20,0.5)(0,0.25) \put(3.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(3.5,1){\line(1,-2){0.5}} \put(3.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.65,0.9){$v_{i}$} \put(3,0){\line(1,0){1}} \put(3,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(4,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(2.7,-0.3){$u_{i}$} \put(3.7,-0.3){$w_{i}$} \put(5,0.5){\vector(1,0){1}} \put(7.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(7.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(7.65,0.9){$v_{i}$} \put(7,0){\line(1,0){1.5}} \put(7,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.5,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(6.7,-0.3){$u_{i}$} \put(7.7,-0.3){$w_{i}$} \put(8.3,-0.3){$x_{i}$} \put(8.5,0){\line(1,0){0.2}} \put(8.8,0){\line(1,0){0.2}} \put(8.5,0){\line(2,1){0.4}} \put(8.5,0){\line(2,-1){0.4}} \end{picture} \caption{Constructing a vertex of degree $1$ in Stage $3a$.} \end{figure} \ Stage $3b$ (If $u_{i}w_{i}$ $
otin E(G)$): \ If $u_{i}w_{i}$ is not an edge in $G$, then insert an edge between $u_{i}$ and $w_{i}$ (this can be done arbitrarily close to the edges $u_{i}v_{i}$ and $v_{i}w_{i}$, so planarity is maintained). Delete the edge $v_{i}w_{i}$. Let $x_{i}$ denote the neighbour of $u_{i}$ that is not $v_{i}$ or $w_{i}$ and let $B_{i} = B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i}, x_{i} \}$.  egin{figure} [ht] \setlength{\unitlength}{1cm}  egin{picture}(20,2.75)(0,0.5) \put(4,3){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(4,3){\line(1,-2){0.5}} \put(3.5,2){\line(0,-1){1}} \put(4,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.9,3.2){$v_{i}$} \put(3.5,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.1,2){$u_{i}$} \put(4.5,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(4.6,2){$w_{i}$} \put(3.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.1,1){$x_{i}$} \put(3.5,1){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(3.5,0.5){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(3.5,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.8,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.2,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(5.5,1.5){\vector(1,0){1}} \put(8.5,3){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(8,2){\line(0,-1){1}} \put(8,2){\line(1,0){1}} \put(8.5,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.4,3.2){$v_{i}$} \put(8,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(7.6,2){$u_{i}$} \put(9,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(9.1,2){$w_{i}$} \put(8,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(7.6,1){$x_{i}$} \put(8,1){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8,0.5){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8.3,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(7.7,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \end{picture} \caption{Constructing a vertex of degree $1$ in Stage $3b$.} \end{figure} \ Stage $4$: \ If $i = \lceil  eta n ceil$, then we terminate the algorithm. Otherwise, we increase $i$ by $1$ and return to Stage $2$. \ Note that we have $d(v_{i}) = 1$ $ orall i$ in our new graph. At each iteration, we had $|A-B_{i-1}| \geq (1 - 9 \epsilon - 6  eta - 8 \delta)n - 6  eta n =(1- 9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta)n$ choices for $v_{i}$. Thus, by considering all possible initial graphs $G \in \mathcal{J}_{n}$, we have at least $(1- 9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta)^{\lceil  eta n ceil} n^{\lceil  eta n ceil}  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$ ways to construct a graph with $\geq  eta n$ vertices of degree $1$, and so it remains only to consider the amount of double-counting. Each new graph will contain at most $3 \lceil  eta n ceil$ vertices of degree $1$ (since there were $< \lceil  eta n ceil$ to begin with; we have deliberately created $\lceil  eta n ceil$; and we may have created at most one extra one each time we used Stage $3a$, if $x_{i}$ was an isolated vertex). Thus, we have $\leq 3 \lceil  eta n ceil$ possibilities for which vertex was $v_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$, which will now be adjacent only to $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$. If $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ now has degree $2$, then we must have used Stage $3a$ in the final iteration and hence $w_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ is the other neighbour of $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ and $x_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ is the remaining neighbour of $w_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$. Thus, we know how the graph changed during the final iteration. If $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ now has degree $3$, then we must have used Stage $3b$ in the final iteration and hence we have two possibilities for which vertex was $w_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ (since it must be one of the other neighbours of $u_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ in the new graph). Thus, we have two possibilities for how the graph changed during the final iteration. Therefore, we have at most $6 \lceil  eta n ceil$ possibilities in total for which vertex was $v_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ and how the graph looked before the final iteration. Repeating this argument, we find that we have at most $\left( 6 \lceil  eta n ceil ight)^{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ possibilities for what the original graph was and which vertices were $v_{1},v_{2}, \ldots, v_{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ (in order). Hence, we have built each of our new graphs at most $(6 \lceil  eta n ceil)^{\lceil  eta n ceil}$ times and, therefore, the number of graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with $\geq  eta n$ vertices of degree $1$ is at least $ \left (  rac{(1-9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta)n}{6 \lceil  eta n ceil} ight) ^{\lceil  eta n ceil}  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$. Recall that $\delta < 1/8$. Thus, since we were free to choose $\epsilon$ and $ eta$ arbitrarily small, we may assume that $ \left (  rac{1-9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta}{6  eta} ight) >3$. Therefore, for sufficiently large~$n$, we have $ \left (  rac{(1-9 \epsilon - 12  eta - 8 \delta)n}{6 \lceil  eta n ceil} ight) ^{\lceil  eta n ceil}  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| > 3^{\lceil  eta n ceil}  rac{e^{- eta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| > |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$, which provides us with a contradiction.

nodes.name: Start from G in J_n
nodes.statement: Suppose instead that $|\mathcal{J}_{n}| \geq \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$ and consider a graph $G \in \mathcal{J}_{n}$. We shall start by showing the intuitive fact that $G$ must contain many vertices of degree $2$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $G\in\mathcal{J}_n$; show it has many degree-2 vertices.

nodes.name: Many degree-2 vertices
Degree-sum inequality (1)
nodes.statement:
d_{1} + 2d_{2} + 3 \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} & \leq & \sum_{i \geq 1}id_{i} 
onumber \ & = & 2m 
onumber \ & \leq & 2n +2\delta n 
onumber \ & = & 2d_{0} + 2d_{1} + 2d_{2} + 2 \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} + 2\delta n.
nodes.label: eq:label1

nodes.name: Bound on high-degree vertices (2)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} & \leq & 2d_{0} + d_{1} + 2\delta n \nonumber \\ & < & 2 \epsilon n + \beta n + 2\delta n
nodes.label: eq:label2

nodes.name: Many degree-2 vertices with degree-2 neighbours
nodes.statement: We shall now see that, in fact, $G$ must contain many vertices of degree~$2$ that are adjacent only to other vertices of degree $2$. Recall from (\ref{eq:label1}) that we have $\sum_{i \geq 1}id_{i} \leq 2d_{0} + 2d_{1} + 2d_{2} + 2 \sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} +~2\delta n$. Thus, \begin{eqnarray*} \sum_{i \geq 3}id_{i} & \leq & 2d_{0} + d_{1} + 2\sum_{i \geq 3}d_{i} + 2\delta n \\ & < & 2 \epsilon n + \beta n + 2(2 \epsilon n + \beta n + 2\delta n) + 2 \delta n \phantom{www} \textrm{ by (\ref{eq:label2})} \\ & = & (6 \epsilon + 3 \beta + 6 \delta)n. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, at most $(6 \epsilon + 3 \beta + 6 \delta)n$ of the degree $2$ vertices will be adjacent to a vertex of degree $\geq 3$. Similarly, at most $d_{1} < \beta n$ of the degree $2$ vertices will be adjacent to a vertex of degree $1$. Hence, at least $d_{2} - \beta n - (6 \epsilon +3 \beta + 6 \delta)n > (1- 3 \epsilon - 2 \beta - 2 \delta)n - \beta n - (6 \epsilon + 3 \beta + 6 \delta)n = (1-9 \epsilon - 6 \beta - 8\delta)n$ of the degree~$2$ vertices will be adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices.
nodes.statement_short: Most degree-2 vertices have only degree-2 neighbours.

nodes.name: Set A and the construction
nodes.statement: Let $A$ denote the set of vertices of degree $2$ that are adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices. Using $G$, we shall construct a graph (in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$) with $ \geq \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$ by the following algorithm:
nodes.statement_short: Define $A$ and construct new graphs by the following stages.

nodes.name: Stage 1: initialise
nodes.statement: Stage $1$: \\ Let $B_{0} = \emptyset$ and let $i=1$.

nodes.name: Stage 2: choose v_i
nodes.statement: Stage $2$: \\ Choose a vertex, $v_{i}$, in $A-B_{i-1}$ (it will become clear that $v_{i}$ will still be a degree $2$ vertex that is adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices). Let the vertices adjacent to $v_{i}$ be denoted by $u_{i}$ and $w_{i}$.

nodes.name: Stage 3a: triangle component
nodes.statement: Stage $3a$ (If $u_{i}w_{i}$ $\in E(G)$): \\ If $u_{i}w_{i}$ is an edge in $G$ (in which case $\{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i} \}$ form a component that is a triangle, since $d(u_{i}) = d(v_{i}) = d(w_{i}) =2$), then delete the edge $v_{i}w_{i}$ and join $w_{i}$ to a vertex $x_{i} \notin (B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i} \} )$ (see Figure~\ref{fig3a}). This is possible if $i \leq \lceil \beta n \rceil$, since it will become clear that $|B_{i-1}| + 2 \leq 6(i-1) +2 <6( \lceil \beta n \rceil -1) +2 < n$ if $\beta < \frac{1}{6}$. Planarity will be maintained, since $w_{i}$ and $x_{i}$ were in separate components. If $d(x_{i}) \neq 2$, let $B_{i} = B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i} \}$. If $d(x_{i}) = 2$, let the vertices adjacent to $x_{i}$ be denoted by $y_{i}$ and $z_{i}$ and let $B_{i} = B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i}, x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i} \}$. Thus, as already mentioned, it is clear that $|B_{i}|$ increases by at most $6$ in each iteration and that $A-B_{i}$ still just contains degree $2$ vertices that are adjacent only to other degree $2$ vertices. \begin{figure} [ht] \setlength{\unitlength}{1cm} \begin{picture}(20,0.5)(0,0.25) \put(3.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(3.5,1){\line(1,-2){0.5}} \put(3.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.65,0.9){$v_{i}$} \put(3,0){\line(1,0){1}} \put(3,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(4,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(2.7,-0.3){$u_{i}$} \put(3.7,-0.3){$w_{i}$} \put(5,0.5){\vector(1,0){1}} \put(7.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(7.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(7.65,0.9){$v_{i}$} \put(7,0){\line(1,0){1.5}} \put(7,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.5,0){\circle*{0.1}} \put(6.7,-0.3){$u_{i}$} \put(7.7,-0.3){$w_{i}$} \put(8.3,-0.3){$x_{i}$} \put(8.5,0){\line(1,0){0.2}} \put(8.8,0){\line(1,0){0.2}} \put(8.5,0){\line(2,1){0.4}} \put(8.5,0){\line(2,-1){0.4}} \end{picture} \caption{Constructing a vertex of degree $1$ in Stage $3a$.} \end{figure}
nodes.statement_short: If $u_iw_i$ is an edge, move $v_iw_i$ to $w_ix_i$.

nodes.name: Stage 3b: longer path
nodes.statement: Stage $3b$ (If $u_{i}w_{i}$ $\notin E(G)$): \\ If $u_{i}w_{i}$ is not an edge in $G$, then insert an edge between $u_{i}$ and $w_{i}$ (this can be done arbitrarily close to the edges $u_{i}v_{i}$ and $v_{i}w_{i}$, so planarity is maintained). Delete the edge $v_{i}w_{i}$. Let $x_{i}$ denote the neighbour of $u_{i}$ that is not $v_{i}$ or $w_{i}$ and let $B_{i} = B_{i-1} \cup \{ u_{i}, v_{i}, w_{i}, x_{i} \}$. \begin{figure} [ht] \setlength{\unitlength}{1cm} \begin{picture}(20,2.75)(0,0.5) \put(4,3){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(4,3){\line(1,-2){0.5}} \put(3.5,2){\line(0,-1){1}} \put(4,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.9,3.2){$v_{i}$} \put(3.5,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.1,2){$u_{i}$} \put(4.5,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(4.6,2){$w_{i}$} \put(3.5,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(3.1,1){$x_{i}$} \put(3.5,1){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(3.5,0.5){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(3.5,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.8,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.5,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(3.2,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(5.5,1.5){\vector(1,0){1}} \put(8.5,3){\line(-1,-2){0.5}} \put(8,2){\line(0,-1){1}} \put(8,2){\line(1,0){1}} \put(8.5,3){\circle*{0.1}} \put(8.4,3.2){$v_{i}$} \put(8,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(7.6,2){$u_{i}$} \put(9,2){\circle*{0.1}} \put(9.1,2){$w_{i}$} \put(8,1){\circle*{0.1}} \put(7.6,1){$x_{i}$} \put(8,1){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8,0.5){\line(0,-1){0.4}} \put(8,1){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8.3,0.4){\line(1,-2){0.2}} \put(8,1){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \put(7.7,0.4){\line(-1,-2){0.2}} \end{picture} \caption{Constructing a vertex of degree $1$ in Stage $3b$.} \end{figure}

nodes.name: Stage 4: iterate
nodes.statement: Stage $4$: \\ If $i = \lceil \beta n \rceil$, then we terminate the algorithm. Otherwise, we increase $i$ by $1$ and return to Stage $2$.

nodes.name: Count constructions
nodes.statement: Note that we have $d(v_{i}) = 1$ $\forall i$ in our new graph. At each iteration, we had $|A-B_{i-1}| \geq (1 - 9 \epsilon - 6 \beta - 8 \delta)n - 6 \beta n =(1- 9 \epsilon - 12 \beta - 8 \delta)n$ choices for $v_{i}$. Thus, by considering all possible initial graphs $G \in \mathcal{J}_{n}$, we have at least $(1- 9 \epsilon - 12 \beta - 8 \delta)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} n^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$ ways to construct a graph with $\geq \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$, and so it remains only to consider the amount of double-counting.

nodes.name: Bound double counting
nodes.statement: Each new graph will contain at most $3 \lceil \beta n \rceil$ vertices of degree $1$ (since there were $< \lceil \beta n \rceil$ to begin with; we have deliberately created $\lceil \beta n \rceil$; and we may have created at most one extra one each time we used Stage $3a$, if $x_{i}$ was an isolated vertex). Thus, we have $\leq 3 \lceil \beta n \rceil$ possibilities for which vertex was $v_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$, which will now be adjacent only to $u_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$. If $u_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ now has degree $2$, then we must have used Stage $3a$ in the final iteration and hence $w_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ is the other neighbour of $u_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ and $x_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ is the remaining neighbour of $w_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$. Thus, we know how the graph changed during the final iteration. If $u_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ now has degree $3$, then we must have used Stage $3b$ in the final iteration and hence we have two possibilities for which vertex was $w_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ (since it must be one of the other neighbours of $u_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ in the new graph). Thus, we have two possibilities for how the graph changed during the final iteration. Therefore, we have at most $6 \lceil \beta n \rceil$ possibilities in total for which vertex was $v_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ and how the graph looked before the final iteration. Repeating this argument, we find that we have at most $\left( 6 \lceil \beta n \rceil \right)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ possibilities for what the original graph was and which vertices were $v_{1},v_{2}, \ldots, v_{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ (in order). Hence, we have built each of our new graphs at most $(6 \lceil \beta n \rceil)^{\lceil \beta n \rceil}$ times and, therefore, the number of graphs in $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$ with $\geq \beta n$ vertices of degree $1$ is at least $ \left ( \frac{(1-9 \epsilon - 12 \beta - 8 \delta)n}{6 \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right) ^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct iterations backwards: at most $(6\lceil\beta n\rceil)^{\lceil\beta n\rceil}$ preimages.

nodes.name: Recall delta < 1/8
nodes.statement: Recall that $\delta < 1/8$.

nodes.name: Contradiction in case (b)
nodes.statement: Thus, since we were free to choose $\epsilon$ and $\beta$ arbitrarily small, we may assume that $ \left ( \frac{1-9 \epsilon - 12 \beta - 8 \delta}{6 \beta} \right) >3$. Therefore, for sufficiently large~$n$, we have $ \left ( \frac{(1-9 \epsilon - 12 \beta - 8 \delta)n}{6 \lceil \beta n \rceil} \right) ^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| > 3^{\lceil \beta n \rceil} \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2} |\mathcal{P}(n,m)| > |\mathcal{P}(n,m)|$, which provides us with a contradiction.

nodes.name: Both cases contradict
nodes.statement: Thus, we get a contradiction whether $\frac{|\mathcal{H}_{n}|}{|\mathcal{P}(n,m)|} \geq \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2}$ or $\frac{|\mathcal{J}_{n}|}{|\mathcal{P}(n,m)|} \geq \frac{e^{-\beta n}}{2}$.

nodes.name: Linearly many pendant edges
nodes.statement: Let $b>0$ and $B<3$ be given constants and let $m(n) \in [bn,Bn]$ for all large $n$. Then there exists a constant $\alpha(b,B) > 0$ such that \begin{displaymath} \mathbf{P}[P_{n,m} \textrm{ will have } < \alpha n \textrm{ pendant edges }] < e^{- \alpha n} \textrm{ for all large } n. \end{displaymath}
nodes.statement_short: If $bn\le m\le Bn$ with $b>0$, $B<3$, then $P_{n,m}$ has $\ge\alpha n$ pendant edges with probability $1-e^{-\alpha n}$.
conclusions: \mathbf{P}[P_{n,m} \textrm{ will have } < \alpha n \textrm{ pendant edges }] < e^{- \alpha n} \textrm{ for all large } n.

nodes.name: Addable non-edge and add(n,m)
nodes.statement: Given a planar graph $G$, we call a non-edge $e$ \emph{\textbf{addable}} in $G$ if the graph $G+e$ obtained by adding $e$ as an edge is still planar. We let \emph{\textbf{add(}$\mathbf{G}$\textbf{)}} denote the set of addable non-edges of $G$ (note that the graph obtained by adding all the edges in \emph{add}$(G)$ may well not be planar) and we let \emph{\textbf{add(}$\mathbf{n,m}$\textbf{)}} denote the minimum value of $|\emph{add}(G)|$ over all graphs $G \in \mathcal{P}(n,m)$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-edge is addable in planar $G$ if adding it keeps planarity; add$(G)$ is their set and add$(n,m)$ its minimum size over $\mathcal{P}(n,m)$.

nodes.name: Lower bound on add(n,m) for m<n
nodes.statement: Let $m=m(n)$. Then \begin{displaymath} \emph{add}(n,m) \geq \frac{(n+m)(n-m-1)}{2}. \end{displaymath}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 18
nodes.statement: Let $G \in \mathcal{P}(n,m)$. Clearly, $G$ must have at least $n-m$ components, and we know that any non-edge between two vertices in different components is addable. Note that the number of possible edges between disjoint sets $X$ and $Y$ is $|X||Y|$ and that if $|X| \leq |Y|$ then $|X||Y| > (|X|-1)(|Y|+1)$. Hence, it follows that the number of addable edges between vertices in different components is minimized when we have $\kappa(G)-1$ isolated vertices and one component of $n- \kappa(G)+1$ vertices. Thus, \begin{eqnarray*} |\textrm{add}(G)| & \geq & \left(^{\kappa(G)-1}_{\phantom{ww}2}\right) + (\kappa(G)-1)(n-\kappa(G)+1) \\ & = & \frac{(\kappa(G)-1)(\kappa(G)-2)}{2} + (\kappa(G)-1)(n- \kappa(G)+1) \\ & = & (\kappa(G)-1) \left( n - \frac{\kappa(G)}{2} \right). \end{eqnarray*} By differentiation, it can be seen that taking $\kappa(G)$ to be $n-m$ minimizes $(\kappa(G)-1) \left( n - \frac{\kappa(G)}{2} \right)$ in the region $\kappa(G) \in [n-m,n]$. Thus, $|\textrm{add}(G)| \geq (n-m-1) \left( n - \frac{n-m}{2} \right) = \frac{(n+m)(n-m-1)}{2}$. \phantom{qwerty} \setlength{\unitlength}{.25cm} \begin{picture}(1,1) \put(0,0){\line(1,0){1}} \put(0,0){\line(0,1){1}} \put(1,1){\line(-1,0){1}} \put(1,1){\line(0,-1){1}} \end{picture} \\ \\ Lemma~\ref{add33} provides us with the lower bound for the first of our four main results from Table~\ref{addsum1}:
nodes.statement_short: Edges between different components are addable; minimise over component structures, extreme case: isolated vertices plus one big component.

nodes.statement: Let $G \in \mathcal{P}(n,m)$. Clearly, $G$ must have at least $n-m$ components, and we know that any non-edge between two vertices in different components is addable.

nodes.name: Asymptotics of add(n,cn)
nodes.statement: Let $c \in (1,3]$ and suppose that $m\!=\!m(n)\!=\!cn +~\!O(1)$ as $n \to \infty$. Then \begin{displaymath} \emph{add}(n,m)=\mu(c)n+O(1), \end{displaymath} where $\mu(c)$, given explicitly in \cite{ger2}, satisfies $\mu(3)=0$, $\mu(c)>0$~$\forall c<3$ and $\mu(c) \to \infty$ as $c \to 1$.
